title: The Father Vindicates the Suffering Son
english: … is the will of him who sent me, “that of all that he has given me I should lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). So, to win life for those who believe in him, he did not refuse insults, or whips, or the trial of being spat upon, though he is God by nature and true Lord.

Then he says, as a man: “And the Lord became my helper; therefore I was not put to shame, but I set my face like a solid rock, and I knew that I would not be ashamed, because he who justifies me draws near” (Isaiah 50:7-8). So he speaks in a human way, as I said, and in no way out of keeping with the measures of his self-emptying.

Yet through these words he seems to hint at the judgment that came down on them for their impiety toward him. For he says, “The Lord became my helper.” It is as if he said: When I had given my back to whips and my cheeks to blows (Isaiah 50:6), and had suffered the sufferings on the cross as well, the Father became my helper. For he came to his defense, and did not allow his own Son to be utterly disgraced, nor indeed to be put to shame. For those who dared to fight against God have been punished, and have paid the penalty for their offenses against me.

By adding, “He who justifies me draws near,” he again deftly made plain that the judgment on those who had outraged him would not be far off or put off, but would come near, as it were, and follow close on the heels of their deeds.

We say that the Son was justified in this way. Since they dared to kill him, though he was righteous and in no way guilty of any fault, they have been punished, as I said; and the punishment of those who suffered it has borne witness that he whom they so impiously outraged was wholly blameless. God the Father said something of this kind: “And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death” (Isaiah 53:9).

By the rich and wicked he means the leaders of the Jews. For they were sick with an extreme love of money, and through it they were carried away into their wickedness against him. Indeed, although they had recognized him, they kept saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance for ourselves” (Matthew 21:38).
“Who is the one who contends with me? Let him stand up against me together. Who is the one who contends with me? Let him come near to me” (Isaiah 50:8).

That he was righteous and wholly innocent (for he committed no sin; 1 Peter 2:22), and yet endured the drunken outrages of the Jews, the divine prophet himself will confirm when he says of him, “See how the righteous one has perished, and no one takes it to heart” (Isaiah 57:1); and again, as in the person of the Jews, speaking of him: “Let us bind the righteous one, for he is troublesome to us” (Isaiah 3:10). The fact itself would proclaim it aloud. For the divine and pure nature of the Word …

title: The New Law Written on the Heart
english: … concerning his own coming, which took place in this world with flesh: “In that time, says the Lord, I will put my laws into their mind, and I will write them on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10). The all-wise Paul rightly understood this too, and writes, saying to those who had received it, “You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God” (2 Corinthians 3:2-3).

So, “Hear me,” he says, that is, receive my words, and do not become unruly as Israel did, clinging to the oldness of the letter of the Law and seeing nothing beyond the types. The commandment given through Moses was laid down “until the time of reformation,” he says (Hebrews 9:10). But since the time of the incarnation is no longer awaited, but is already here, let the shadow give way to the truth.

“Hear me, then, my people” (Isaiah 51:4). In saying “my people,” he holds out to them the spiritual kinship granted to them in due time. By this too, I think, he puts them to shame, and makes them more eager to accept the word that comes from him.

He calls not only those who belong among the peoples, but kings along with them, so that you may understand the rulers, that is, the leaders of the peoples. For many were brought to this rank from the multitude of believers, and the divine disciples were their firstfruits. Then those who followed after them in their footsteps were given the name of kingship, since they were rich in the name of kingship and were also appointed to lead the peoples.

And so, as if from very great joy, they lift up songs of thanksgiving to God, saying, “He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet” (Psalm 47:3). The divine Psalmist also sings of them: “The rulers of the peoples were gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 47:9).
“O peoples and kings,” he says, “hear me and give ear,” and learn what is promised for the time to come. “A law will go out from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations” (Isaiah 51:4).

Here he calls the divine Gospel proclamation a law. For the new and saving decree is of another kind, as it were; yet it is, as it were, a change of the old law for the better, and a passing over of the types, which have run their course, into the truth. So Christ said, “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For I tell you, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things take place” (Matthew 5:17-18).

But the law in letters was given through Moses, while the saving proclamation, that is, the Gospel, went out through Christ (compare John 1:17). For it was fitting that Moses should become the minister of the shadow and the type, as it seems, of knowledge and of true worship …

title: I Am He Who Comforts You
english: … washing away of sin, that is, the washing that comes through faith in Christ. Where there is the supply and grace of the Holy Spirit, the honor of adoption, the enjoyment of unending good things, and the hope of the kingdom of heaven, there surely we must rejoice, and pain, grief, and groaning have fled away (Isaiah 51:11). For what place will pain have, and over what could there be groaning, where there is no cause at all for groaning and pain, but rather hope prevails, hope of exultation and gladness, of delight that cannot be lost, and of joy?

“I am, I am he who comforts you. Know who you are, that you were afraid of a mortal man and of a son of man, who have withered like grass. And you forgot God who made you, who made heaven and founded the earth, and you were always afraid, all the days, of the face of him who afflicts you. For just as he planned to take you away, so now where is the fury of him who afflicts you? For in your being saved he will not stop, nor will he delay” (Isaiah 51:12-14).

Here “I am” means “I live and exist”; for he himself is He Who Is (Exodus 3:14). This is a title fitting for God and surpassing all others. For being and living belong only to the nature that is beyond all things, which did not receive them from another by participation, nor holds them as a gift, but rather is itself life.

So he says, “I am he who comforts you,” that is, he who gives every spiritual comfort, and holds you up with his help so that you stand firmly fixed, ready to go with courage straight toward every virtue. Or perhaps you will understand the comfort here in another way too. For through the Gospel proclamations the Savior was calling people to the washing away of sin through faith in him, I mean, to a share in the Holy Spirit, and to the boast and glory of adoption.

But you, O Israel, he says, did not stand in awe of me, who am, but looked down on me and despised him who calls you to life; yet you were afraid of a perishable man and of a son of man, who have withered like grass. Then you forgot God who made you, who fashioned heaven and established the earth, and you feared the face of him who afflicts you.

Here God accuses the leaders of the Jews, who persisted to the end in opposing the Savior's glory, and, as far as it lay with them, declared it to be nothing at all. He worked wonders in many ways, but they poured out astonishingly bitter words on his divine signs; for they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons (Matthew 12:24).
